title: Glory on the Mountain, Lessons Below
overview: Three of Jesus' followers glimpse his glory on a mountain, and then he frees a suffering boy, again predicts his death, and teaches that true greatness means serving the least.

parts.label: A glimpse of glory (vv. 1-8)
parts.note: Jesus shines with light while Moses and Elijah, often read as standing for Israel's Law and Prophets, talk with him, and many readers see this as a first fulfillment of the promise in verse 1. Peter wants to build shelters to hold on to the moment, but a voice from the cloud calls Jesus God's Son and tells them to listen to him.

parts.label: Waiting for Elijah (vv. 9-13)
parts.note: Based on the book of Malachi, religious teachers expected the prophet Elijah to return before God set things right. Jesus says Elijah has already come and been mistreated, which is widely understood to mean John the Baptist, who was executed (Mark 6).

parts.label: A father's mixed faith (vv. 14-29)
parts.note: To many modern readers the boy's seizures sound like epilepsy, though Mark describes a spirit, and the father's cry holds trust and doubt together. Jesus says this kind comes out only by prayer but does not explain further, and some later manuscripts add 'and fasting.'

parts.label: Who is the greatest (vv. 30-37)
parts.note: Right after Jesus again predicts his death and rising, his followers argue about rank. He places a child among them, someone with almost no status then, and says that welcoming such a person is welcoming him and God.

parts.label: Not one of us (vv. 38-41)
parts.note: The disciples try to stop a man who drives out demons in Jesus' name because he is not part of their group. Jesus tells them not to, saying whoever is not against them is for them, and that even a cup of water given to his followers will be rewarded.

parts.label: Stumbling, fire and salt (vv. 42-50)
parts.note: Cutting off a hand or tearing out an eye is widely read as deliberate exaggeration about taking wrongdoing seriously, and the word for hell names a valley outside Jerusalem linked with burning, while verse 48 quotes Isaiah 66:24. The salt sayings are hard to pin down; scholars connect them to salt as a preservative or to the salt added to sacrifices, but the exact sense is unsure.

disagreement: Christians differ on what Jesus meant in verse 1 when he said some would see God's kingdom come with power, reading it as the transfiguration that follows, his resurrection and the spread of the early church, or the fall of Jerusalem in 70 AD.
think: Have you ever trusted something and doubted it at the same time, and how did you live with both?
